summary: Defines Augmented BNF, a compact notation for writing the syntax of protocols and message formats. It separates this definition out of the early email specifications so that others can cite it, with some changes and additions. It was replaced by RFC 4234.

eli5.summary: It is a way of writing rules for what a message must look like, such as which parts come first, like a grammar for computers.

questions: how to write protocol syntax rules
how do abnf repetition operators work
what is the difference between abnf and bnf
subtitle: A compact notation for writing down the exact syntax of protocol messages.

tldr.problem: Internet specifications often need to define a format syntax, and each one used whatever notation its authors liked. The email specifications carried their own copy of the Augmented BNF definition that others kept citing.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2234 pulls that definition out into its own document. It defines rule naming, terminal values and a small set of operators for alternatives, repetition, grouping and options, then defines ABNF in ABNF itself.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2234 has been obsoleted by RFC 4234, so new work should cite the newer document.

today: RFC 2234 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4234, which should be cited instead.

sections.title: Why ABNF Was Split Out
sections.content:
A modified version of Backus-Naur Form (BNF), called Augmented BNF (ABNF), had been popular among many Internet specifications. The RFC says it balances compactness and simplicity, with reasonable representational power.

In the early days of the Arpanet, each specification contained its own definition of ABNF, including the email specifications RFC 733 and then RFC 822. This document separates the definition out so that it can be referenced selectively, and adds some modifications and enhancements. The differences from standard BNF involve naming rules, repetition, alternatives, order-independence and value ranges.
sections.eli5: Many rulebooks each had their own copy of the same how-to-read-the-rules page. This RFC puts that page in one place so everybody can point to it.

sections.title: Rules, Names and Terminal Values
sections.content:
A rule has the form name = elements crlf. A rule name starts with an alphabetic character followed by letters, digits and hyphens, and names are case-insensitive. Angle brackets are not required, but may be used around a rule name in free-form prose to make it easier to spot.

Rules resolve into strings of terminal values. In ABNF a character is merely a non-negative integer. A value is written with a base letter: b for binary, d for decimal and x for hexadecimal. So CR = %d13 and CR = %x0D mean the same thing, and a period joins values, as in CRLF = %d13.10.

Literal text can be written in quotation marks, and such strings are case-insensitive US-ASCII. To require an exact case, spell the characters out individually, for example %d97.98.99 matches only lowercase abc. How values are encoded on the wire is outside ABNF: the same grammar can have a 7-bit US-ASCII, a binary octet or a 16-bit Unicode encoding.
sections.eli5: Each rule has a name and a recipe. Letters can be written as plain quotes or as secret number codes, and quotes do not care about big or small letters.

sections.title: The Operators
sections.content:
Concatenation lists rule names in order, so mumble = foo bar foo matches aba when foo is %x61 and bar is %x62. ABNF does not allow for white space implicitly: a grammar that wants linear white space around delimiters must say so explicitly.

  • Alternatives: foo / bar accepts either. =/ adds alternatives to an earlier rule in fragments.
  • Value range: DIGIT = %x30-39. A numeric value may use the dotted form or one dash range, not both in the same string.
  • Group: parentheses make a strictly ordered single element.
  • Repetition: <a>*<b>element means at least a and at most b occurrences. The defaults are 0 and infinity, so 1*element requires at least one and 2DIGIT means exactly two digits.
  • Option: [foo bar] is the same as *1(foo bar).
  • Comment: a semicolon runs to the end of the line.

From tightest to loosest binding the order is: strings and names, comment, value range, repetition, grouping and option, concatenation, alternative. The RFC strongly advises using grouping, for example (elem foo) / (bar blat), rather than relying on readers to apply the precedence correctly.
sections.eli5: There are a few little symbols: a slash means one or the other, a star means any number of times, and square brackets mean you can skip it.

sections.title: ABNF Defined in ABNF
sections.content:
Section 4 gives the formal grammar of ABNF written in ABNF, using the core rules of Appendix A. A rulelist is one or more rules or blank or comment lines. A rule is a rulename, a defined-as (either = or =/), its elements and a newline; it continues on the next line if that line starts with white space.

The grammar also pins down the pieces: repeat, group, option, quoted char-val, numeric num-val in binary, decimal or hex, and prose-val, a description in angle brackets that is to be used as a last resort.
sections.eli5: The rulebook for writing rules is itself written using the same kind of rules, like a dictionary that defines the word dictionary.

sections.title: Core Rules and Security
sections.content:
Appendix A supplies core rules as a convenience, separate from the meta language itself. They include ALPHA (%x41-5A / %x61-7A), BIT, CHAR, CR, LF, CRLF, DIGIT, DQUOTE, HEXDIG, HTAB, SP, VCHAR, WSP, OCTET and LWSP. The common encoding is 7-bit US-ASCII in an 8-bit field with the high bit zero, in network byte order.

The security considerations section states only that security is truly believed to be irrelevant to this document.
sections.eli5: There is also a starter kit of ready-made pieces, like letters, digits and spaces, that other rulebooks can borrow.

items.label: Alternative
items.desc: foo / bar accepts foo or bar.

items.label: Incremental alternative
items.desc: Adds alternatives to an existing rule.

items.label: Value range
items.desc: Any single value in the range.

items.label: Group
items.desc: Treats a strictly ordered sequence as one element.

items.label: Variable repetition
items.desc: Optional minimum and maximum count; defaults 0 and infinity.

items.label: Option
items.desc: Same as *1 of the enclosed sequence.

items.label: Comment
items.desc: Runs to the end of the line.
